science.title: Wild bee Lasioglossum malachurum (Hymenoptera: Halictidae) responses to pesticides and urban pollutants: linking cholinesterase activity and morphological traits
science.description: Wild bees are important pollinators. However, their populations are threatened by pesticide exposure and urban pollution. This study examines the effects of environmental pollutants on the wild bee species Lasioglossum malachurum. Cholinesterase (ChE) activity and protein levels were measured as physiological biomarkers, while morphological traits (weights and ratios) were evaluated as alternative anatomical biomarkers of neurotoxicity. Bees were sampled from organic agriculture (reference site), conventional agriculture (pesticide exposure), and urban agriculture (urban pollution). Significant declines in ChE activity and protein content were observed in bees from conventionally managed fields, suggesting pesticide-induced neurotoxicity and impaired protein assimilation. Moreover, morphological alterations, particularly a substantial decrease in both head-to-total and head-to-body ratios, were found to be associated with acetylcholinesterase inhibition. Conversely, bees from urban agriculture exhibited increased body protein content and ChE activity but no significant morphological alterations, indicating an adaptive response to sublethal urban pollutants. Overall, morphological biomarkers showed promise as rapid and practical anatomical indicators of neurotoxicity from pesticide exposure, in accordance with findings of physiological biomarkers. However, their effectiveness was limited in urban environments due to the complexity of urban pollutants. This study highlights the importance of integrating physiological and morphological biomarkers into biomonitoring frameworks, contributing to the development of non-destructive methodologies.

science.title: Delayed brain network energy development in preterm youth impairs cognitive function: evidence from the longitudinal ABCD study
science.description: Preterm birth disrupts early brain development, increasing the risk of cognitive difficulties. However, its long-term effects on functional brain network energy, a metric of large-scale network stability and adaptability, remain poorly understood. Using resting-state fMRI data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, we examined how prematurity influences brain network energy across late childhood and early adolescence. Our sample included 818 preterm-born youth and 2,149 matched full-term controls. Compared to full-term adolescents, preterm individuals exhibited altered multiscale functional connectivity and persistent reductions in functional network energy, specifically within the sensorimotor (SM) and higher-cognitive temporoparietal (HC-TP) networks, at both baseline and 2-year follow-up. These findings suggest diminished functional flexibility and network integration in preterm-born individuals. To further contextualize these results, we incorporated data from 1,633 participants in the Human Connectome Project (HCP) and HCP-Development studies, confirming that network energy increases with age in typically developing youth and is consistently reduced in preterm individuals. Notably, lower energy in the HC-TP network was specifically associated with deficits in crystallized cognition, but not with behavioral problems. Meta-analytic decoding further linked the HC-TP network to language and social cognition, providing a mechanistic explanation for its relationship with crystallized cognitive abilities. These findings highlight the persistence of neurodevelopmental alterations in preterm individuals, particularly affecting higher-order cognitive functions, and position network energy as a potential marker of altered neurodevelopment following preterm birth.
